thread.title: Lack of Trading Volume Tells Me This Correction Is Not Over

author: Jim Collins
title: Lack of Trading Volume Tells Me This Correction Is Not Over
text:
Wow! What a day. Just a series of quick plateaus and a real, old-fashioned stock market sell-off. Nasdaq favorites led this decline and the Nasdaq Composite's 4.08% decline was the worst of the major indices. During the day I was watching prices, as everyone does, but my first check at 4:01 PM was for volume. The Nasdaq must have been rockin' today, right? No, it wasn't, and that tells me there is still pent-up selling pressure. Today's Nasdaq volume, as measured by the FINRA/TRF composite tape, was 2.555 billion shares. That doesn't even place it in the top 10 days for 2018. In fact it was more than 750 million shares below this year's number 10 volume day, March 13th, and a full 2 billion shares below this year's high-water mark, the 4.584 billion shares traded on September 21st.
So, where was everybody? Well, as most know, the Nasdaq is populated by computers, not people, and those algorithms tend to get pumping on options expirations Fridays, as index futures and individual stock cross-trades play out. September 21st was one such day.
Today was just a regular old Wednesday, but with the DJIA down 831 points, I expected more shares to change hands. The volume in the most-watched individual names was elevated, though. The FAANG complex--Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix and Alphabet (parent company of Google)--all saw higher than average volume, and so did Tesla, which I include in the following table because I write about that stock nearly every day.
Stock 10/10 vol.(mm) 10-day avg. vol. (mm) AMZN 10.3 4.8 FB 30.1 27.6 AAPL 40.9 29.0 NFLX 16.5 11.0 GOOG 2,2 1,5 TSLA 12.8 10.4 MCD 4.1 3.4 HD 6.0 4.0 JNJ 6.7 6.1 PG 8.7 7.1 This market has been so FAANG-addled for so long that I don't think group rotation is possible. So, if fund managers were actually selling individual stocks today, not just watching the steering wheel, that bodes ill for stocks. Amazon traded "only" 10.3 million shares today, but that is 2.5x average volume, and really, it is not easy to trade huge lots of a stock that is priced at more than $1,700 per share.
If fund managers truly have lost faith in FAANG, I believe they will reallocate their portfolios toward cash and cash substitutes, not defensive stocks. McDonald's, Home Depot, Procter & Gamble and Johnson & Johnson all fell 1.0% or less today, a classic defensive pattern. As the table shows, however, the volume in those names was not significantly elevated versus recent averages. That convinces me today’s trading action was not full-bore group rotation.
The 3-month Treasury bill is yielding 2.27% today versus the 1.88% yield the S&P 500 sported as of yesterday’s close, so there is a real possibility of substitution.
So, overall market action was not indicative of a day on which the machines ruled the world. No, today it was people, and that is always scarier.
Machines look at the last ten years of data and say how could we robo-managers not overweight stocks, especially the high-flyers; with an intelligence based solely on “1”s and “0”s, the past is always prelude. People, on the other hand, can look at real-world portfolios and decide to take money off the table when cash is an increasingly attractive option.
